2.add: Magnetic influence on orientation was therefore demonstrated in a preparation in which visible landmarks were unavailable and the magnetic field was the controlled variable.

3.add: Its strength is control over a single sensory variable, so a change in heading can be attributed to the magnetic field.

4.add: The horizontal reversal shifts magnetic north by 180°, and experiments that vary inclination test whether the compass depends on the polarity of the field or on the slope of the field lines.

6.add: The different headings at 57°, 60° and 30° show that hatchlings respond to the angle of the field lines, and some inclinations produced no consistent group direction under the same procedure.

7.add: Inclination varies with latitude, so the angle of the field lines could mark approximate position along the migratory route.

8.add: Hatchlings therefore respond to combinations of inclination and intensity that mark regions of the route, with a different heading for each regional field.

third_paragraph.9: The laboratory responses distinguish regional fields without deciding between an inherited map and field-triggered instructions. More sophisticated navigation could develop as turtles mature, and experience-dependent magnetic learning can coexist with early boundary responses.

10.add: The learned response shows that magnetic signatures can serve as cues that predict food.

11.add: Turtle dancing is a behavioral readout of the learned significance of the field, and it can be scored from video by observers who do not know the treatment.

12.add: Recognition extended across pairs that differed in geographical and magnetic separation, and a second pair was learned after the first.

third_paragraph.13: The result establishes that a learned magnetic association can persist for at least four months in captivity. Retention was measured with the same compass-free discrimination task, without further conditioning during the interval.

14.add: Mismatched fields separate the contribution of inclination from that of intensity, so the compound cue can be analyzed into its components.

15.add: The comparison with a stored association could occur in transduction, sensory pathways, memory circuits or the selection of a food-anticipatory action.

16.add: The learned map response persisted with radiofrequency noise, whereas the compass-dependent heading was lost, and the two tasks used different developmental stages and preparations.

17.add: A pulse that changes learned map responses would support a magnetization-based receptor mechanism for the map.

18.add: The initial conditioning result establishes a measurable learned response against which the subsequent perturbation can be assessed, and the controls were completed before the pulse treatment so that a previous pulse could not contaminate them.

third_paragraph.19: Pulse sensitivity supports a candidate class of mechanism, magnetite-containing structures whose magnetic moments a strong pulse could alter. The receptor cells, their connection to a sensory nerve and the ion channel through which a particle might affect membrane voltage are the elements that a complete receptor pathway would include.
third_paragraph.20: Artificial light on a developed beach can compete with orientation cues, and the observational records document how often hatchlings fail to reach the sea. Controlled laboratory experiments with magnetic fields address the sensory basis of a compass, and beach disorientation concerns a separate stage of the journey.

21.add: Perch activation provides a simple orientation measure that is recorded without a free flight.

22.add: An inclination compass reads the axis of the field lines relative to gravity, so reversing both components preserves the information that the bird uses.

third_paragraph.23: The result shows that the directional code of the compass depends on the inclined axis of the field relative to the up–down reference of the bird, and a horizontal field does not supply it.

24.add: Cluster N is therefore a candidate processing region for night vision in migratory songbirds, and its activity can reflect visual sensitivity, magnetic information or other orientation cues.

third_paragraph.25: Cluster N expression was higher at night in migratory species than in non-migratory species, which supports specialization of this region for nocturnal sensory processing. Minimizing recent movement before tissue collection reduced the possibility that flight alone produced the difference.
third_paragraph.26: Eye covering blocks ordinary vision, so the fall in Cluster N activation places the region in a visually dependent processing pathway. More selective tests can then separate magnetic information from other dim-light visual signals.

27.add: Sham-operated birds changed direction with each field manipulation, so the loss of orientation in lesioned birds is attributable to damage to Cluster N and not to the surgery.

28.add: Birds with Cluster N lesions oriented with stars and at sunset, so the deficit is specific to the magnetic compass among the tested orientation behaviors.

29.add: Compass direction and location-related map information are different functions, and this experiment tested the compass and not a displacement correction.

30.add: The birds stay at the capture site, so a heading change reflects the magnetic information alone while celestial, olfactory and landmark cues keep their original values.

31.add: The complementary results come from reed warblers for the map and from robins for the compass.

32.add: Grounding the screens and adding deliberate noise then test whether electromagnetic noise is the variable responsible.

33.add: Field measurements documented the difference in electromagnetic noise between grounded and ungrounded huts, which links the change in orientation to the electromagnetic environment.

34.add: The effects support an electromagnetic sensitivity relevant to compass processing, and independent molecular and anatomical tests evaluate the candidate radical-pair mechanism.

35.add: Seasonal expression of Cry4 correlates with the migratory period, which makes it a candidate for a role in nocturnal navigation.

third_paragraph.36: Localization places the candidate protein in photoreceptor outer segments, a tissue compatible with a visually mediated magnetic process. The staining pattern was examined in robins and chickens with both monoclonal and polyclonal reagents.
third_paragraph.37: Cry4 overlapped iodopsin-positive outer segments, which narrows the candidate cellular location to long-wavelength single cones and double cones. Ordinary photoreceptor identity and a hypothesized magnetic role are separate properties that experiments on function address.

38.add: Reliable molecular localization is a prerequisite for a receptor hypothesis, and the antibody controls make the staining specific for Cry4.

39.add: Cry4 therefore has the cofactor and the electron-transfer chain on which the radical-pair mechanism depends.

40.add: Particular tryptophan residues therefore determine how quickly radicals form and how long they persist.

third_paragraph.41: The measurements establish magnetic sensitivity of the radical chemistry in vitro. Wild-type protein and the tryptophan mutant showed different magnetic field effects, which connects molecular structure to photochemical sensitivity under controlled temperature and chemical conditions.

42.add: Recycling of the protein toward its starting state supports its plausibility as a reusable sensor, with times of about 13 minutes and about 1 minute for the two steps.

43.add: A material sensitive to magnetism must be linked to an identified sensory cell and pathway before it can be considered a receptor, and the iron-positive cells varied strongly across birds.

44.add: The iron-rich clusters examined in the upper beak are therefore immune cells and not magnetosensitive neurons, and the peripheral source of trigeminal magnetic information is a separate question.

45.add: The receptor-to-behavior circuits, including the transmitters and ion channels, connect these candidate mechanisms to behavior.

inserts.title: A compass gives direction and a map gives position
paragraphs: A compass supplies a direction, such as north or the heading to follow. A map supplies information about location, which allows an animal to determine where it is relative to a goal and which way it must go.

Lohmann tested hatchling loggerheads in a harness connected to a freely rotating lever. A rheostat converted the position of the lever into an electrical record of heading, and turtles swam for 90 to 180 min in darkness under the natural field or a reversed horizontal field.

The natural-field group preferred 42° and the reversed-field group preferred 196°. A change in heading with the field shows that hatchlings read direction from the field, which is the function of a compass.
notes: Navigation uses two different kinds of information, direction and position.
Compass.
A compass supplies direction.
It tells the animal which way it is heading.
Map.
A map supplies information related to location.
It tells the animal where it is relative to a goal.
Experiment.
Hatchlings swam in a harness connected to a freely rotating lever.
A rheostat converted lever position into an electrical record of heading.
Conditions.
Turtles swam for 90 to 180 minutes in darkness.
The field was either natural or had a reversed horizontal component.
Result.
The natural-field group preferred 42 degrees.
The reversed-field group preferred 196 degrees.
Meaning.
A heading that follows the field is a compass response, because it reports a direction and not a location.
Why darkness.
Swimming in complete darkness removes visual landmarks, so the field is the available directional cue.
The dim eastern light before the test gave all turtles the same starting experience.
Recording heading.
A harness and lever allow heading to be recorded continuously during swimming.

inserts.title: Polarity and inclination compasses use different information
paragraphs: A polarity compass distinguishes the two ends of a magnetic field line, so it knows which end points toward the magnetic pole. An inclination compass uses the angle at which field lines meet the horizontal and distinguishes poleward from equatorward by the slope of the line.

Reversing the horizontal component of the field changed the preferred swimming course of hatchlings from 42° to 196°. The coil shifted magnetic north by 180° while the vertical component stayed unchanged.

A reversal of the horizontal component alone does not separate the two kinds of compass. Experiments that change inclination while holding field strength constant test which property of the field the turtle uses.
notes: The same behavior can arise from two different compass designs.
Polarity compass.
A polarity compass distinguishes the two directed ends of a magnetic vector.
Inclination compass.
An inclination compass uses the axial slope of the field lines relative to the horizontal.
Poleward is the direction in which the field lines dip more steeply.
The manipulation.
The coil reversed the horizontal component and left the vertical component unchanged.
Magnetic north shifted by 180 degrees.
Field values.
The natural horizontal field was 0.26 oersted.
The reversed field ranged from 0.23 to 0.26 oersted in the swimming zone.
Result.
The preferred heading shifted from 42 to 196 degrees.
Orientation under reversal was more dispersed.
Next test.
Varying inclination at constant intensity separates the slope of the field from its polarity.
Why this does not separate the designs.
Reversing the horizontal component reverses polarity and also reverses the horizontal direction of the field axis.
Both designs predict a change in heading.

inserts.title: Inclination and intensity are separate field properties
paragraphs: Intensity is the magnitude of the magnetic field, and inclination is the angle of the field lines relative to the horizontal. Earth's field varies in both properties with location, but the two can be changed independently in the laboratory. Holding intensity constant isolates the effect of the slope of the field.
Lohmann and Lohmann used two orthogonal coil systems to control the horizontal and vertical components. Total field strength stayed at 0.044 to 0.045 mT across conditions while inclination changed.

Computers and power supplies remained active in every treatment and were located in an adjacent room. Any change in behavior can therefore be attributed to the geometry of the field and not to equipment noise or a change in strength.
notes: Separating two properties of the field allows each to be tested alone.
Definitions.
Intensity is the magnitude of the field.
Inclination is the angle at which field lines intersect the horizontal.
Natural covariation.
In nature both properties change with location.
In the laboratory they can be set separately.
Coils.
Two orthogonal coil systems controlled the horizontal and vertical components independently.
Arena.
Hatchlings swam in a 1.22-meter arena.
A digital encoder recorded heading to the nearest 1.4 degrees every 10 seconds.
Constant strength.
Total field strength was 0.044 to 0.045 millitesla across conditions.
Equipment controls.
Computers and power supplies stayed active in every treatment and sat in an adjacent room.
Why intensity must be constant.
A change in field strength could itself affect behavior.
Holding strength near 0.045 millitesla removes that possibility.
Interpretation.
A change in heading across inclinations therefore reflects the angle of the field lines.
The measured total field strength stayed within a narrow range in every condition.

inserts.title: A magnetic signature combines inclination and intensity
paragraphs: A magnetic signature is the combination of magnetic parameters that characterizes a location. Inclination and intensity vary together across the ocean, so a particular pair of values marks a particular region. The signature of a region is therefore a property of the field at that place.

Lohmann and colleagues replicated three fields from the North Atlantic route of loggerheads and tethered hatchlings in a coil system. Hatchlings oriented east-southeast in the northern Florida field, south in the northeastern gyre field and west-northwest in the southern gyre field.

The animals stayed in the same laboratory arena while the field changed. Each regional signature therefore triggered a different heading, which is consistent with moving toward favorable currents and away from the edges of the gyre.
notes: A location can be recognized from several field properties at once.
Definition.
A magnetic signature is the combination of magnetic parameters characteristic of a location.
Why a combination.
Inclination and intensity vary together across the ocean.
A pair of values is more specific than either value alone.
Fields tested.
Three fields from the North Atlantic route were replicated.
Responses.
East-southeast in the northern Florida field.
South in the northeastern gyre field and west-northwest in the southern gyre field.
Apparatus.
A computerized coil system set the field while the animals stayed in the same arena.
Interpretation.
The headings fit movement into favorable currents and away from displacement beyond the gyre.
Hatchlings had not been to sea.
The tested hatchlings had never entered the ocean, so the responses did not depend on prior travel in those regions.
Routes.
The route is the North Atlantic gyre followed by young loggerheads.
The fields come from locations along that route.

inserts.title: Associative learning links a cue to an outcome
paragraphs: Associative learning is the formation of a link between a sensory cue and an outcome. After a cue has reliably predicted food, the animal shows anticipatory behavior when the cue appears. The behavior is measured in the absence of food, so it reflects memory of the association.

Goforth and colleagues conditioned juvenile loggerheads for 2 months with two replicated geographical fields. Animals spent equal time in the fields, and food was delivered only in one assigned signature, with the rewarded field counterbalanced across animals.

After conditioning, turtles were tested without food and danced more in the rewarded field. Counterbalancing shows that the response follows the association and not a preference for a northern field, a southern field or part of the apparatus. Dancing therefore reports recognition of a magnetic signature.
notes: Learning gives magnetic fields a meaning that the experimenter assigns.
Definition.
Associative learning links a sensory cue with an outcome.
Conditioning.
Juvenile loggerheads were conditioned for 2 months with two replicated geographical fields.
Time spent in the two fields was equal.
Reward.
Food was delivered only in one assigned signature.
Counterbalancing.
Either field could predict food across animals.
This separates a learned association from a fixed preference.
Test.
Turtles were tested without food.
Turtle dancing was scored from video.
Result.
Dancing was longer in the field that had been paired with food.
Behavior scored.
Turtle dancing includes vertical body tilt, the head near or above water, mouth opening and alternating front-flipper movement.
Duration was scored from video recordings.
Blind scoring.
Observers did not know the magnetic treatment.
Turtles danced more in the rewarded signature after equivalent exposure to both.
The output is time spent in a behavioral state and not the direction of swimming.

inserts.title: Mismatched fields test which components matter
paragraphs: Mismatched fields combine the inclination of one learned field with the intensity of the other. Because inclination and intensity normally occur as a pair, the mismatched combinations separate features that were always presented together during training. Mismatched fields were new to the turtles and were not paired with food during training.

Goforth and colleagues tested turtles in the rewarded field, the unrewarded field and the two mismatched combinations. Each mismatched field kept one rewarded component and changed the other. Responses in each condition were scored from the same behavioral measure.

The test asks whether a familiar inclination or a familiar intensity is enough to evoke the learned response. If neither is enough, the learned signature is a compound cue that depends on the combination.
notes: A mismatch separates two features that normally occur together.
Training fields.
Inclination and intensity varied together during conditioning.
Mismatched fields.
One mismatched field combined the inclination of one learned field with the intensity of the other.
The second mismatched field reversed this pairing.
Test conditions.
Turtles were tested in the rewarded field, the unrewarded field and both mismatched fields.
Question.
The test asks whether a familiar inclination or a familiar intensity alone is sufficient.
Possible outcomes.
A response to a mismatched field would show that one component is sufficient.
No response would show that the combination is needed.
Compound cue.
A signature can function as a compound cue and not as a single coordinate.
Possible readouts.
If turtles danced in a mismatched field, one component would be sufficient.
If they did not dance, both components would be needed.
Compound signature.
A signature can act as a compound cue, which is not a single coordinate.

inserts.title: A dissociation shows that two tasks use different mechanisms
paragraphs: A dissociation occurs when a manipulation changes one behavior and leaves another unchanged. It suggests that the two behaviors rely on different mechanisms. The same class of perturbation was tested against two different behavioral outputs.

Goforth and colleagues exposed turtles to broadband radiofrequency noise from 0.1 to 10 MHz. The learned rewarded-field response persisted, whereas hatchlings exposed to the Cape Verde signature lost their group heading. Hatchlings were oriented in a harness and their heading was recorded.

Without noise, the hatchlings preferred 293.1°, approximately westward, and with noise the group no longer shared a direction. The map-only assay and the orientation task requiring map and compass information therefore respond differently to the same perturbation. Selective loss of one behavior shows that it depends on a process that the noise disrupts.
notes: A selective effect of a manipulation points to separate mechanisms.
Definition.
A dissociation is a change in one behavior with another behavior spared.
Manipulation.
Radiofrequency fields are rapidly oscillating electromagnetic fields.
Broadband noise spanned 0.1 to 10 megahertz.
Map-only assay.
The learned rewarded-field response persisted with the noise.
Orientation task.
Hatchlings exposed to the Cape Verde signature lost a consistent group heading with noise.
Without noise they preferred 293.1 degrees.
Interpretation.
Different mechanisms may contribute to the map and to the compass.
Preparations.
The two tasks used different developmental stages, so the comparison is between behaviors and not between receptors in one animal.
Radiofrequency fields.
These are rapidly oscillating electromagnetic fields.
They are used as a perturbation that may disturb radical-pair processes.
Interpretation.
The map and the compass may use different mechanisms.
The result does not name either mechanism.
Only the compass-dependent task lost its group heading under the noise.

inserts.title: Magnetite and radical pairs make different predictions
paragraphs: Magnetite is an iron oxide whose particles have a magnetic moment, so a strong pulse can change their arrangement or magnetization. A radical-pair reaction is a chemical process that is influenced by a field only while it is present.

Mackiewicz and colleagues gave turtles a magnetic pulse lasting 5 ms with a maximum of 85 mT. Turtles danced less in their rewarded field after the pulse than after no pulse, and sham handling did not produce the reduction.

A persistent effect of a brief pulse fits a particle-based mechanism better than a radical-pair mechanism. The result therefore supports magnetite-containing structures as a candidate for the map while the receptor itself has not been located.
notes: The two main receptor hypotheses behave differently after a strong pulse.
Magnetite.
Magnetite is an iron oxide that can interact with magnetic fields.
A pulse can alter its magnetic arrangement.
Radical pair.
A radical-pair reaction depends on the field while it is present.
A brief pulse is not expected to leave a persistent change.
Pulse.
The pulse lasted 5 milliseconds and reached 85 millitesla.
That is far stronger than Earth-strength fields.
Controls.
No-pulse, sham-pulse and actual-pulse treatments were compared.
Sham handling did not cause the reduction.
Result.
Turtles danced less in the rewarded field after the pulse.
Directions.
Pulses parallel and antiparallel to the horizontal Earth field were considered together.
Why direction of the pulse did not matter.
Pulses parallel and antiparallel to the horizontal field did not produce distinguishable responses and were treated together.
Controls.
Sham animals were handled in the magnetizer without a pulse.
Observers scoring video did not know the treatment.

inserts.title: Immediate-early genes mark recently active neurons
paragraphs: ZENK is an immediate-early gene whose expression rises in neurons shortly after they are activated. Measuring its product in tissue sections reveals which regions were recruited during a behavior. The measure is applied to brain sections after the birds have been exposed to the condition.

Mouritsen and colleagues exposed migratory garden warblers and European robins and non-migratory zebra finches and canaries to dim light of 0.04 lux or to ordinary daytime light. A dorsal forebrain region called Cluster N showed strong night-time expression in migrants. The dim light approximated moonlight.
The measure integrates activity over time and is not an instantaneous spike record. It therefore identifies a candidate region that is recruited during night vision in migratory birds.
notes: A molecular marker can show where the brain was active during an experience.
Marker.
ZENK is an immediate-early transcriptional marker whose expression changes with neuronal activation.
Species.
Migratory garden warblers and European robins were compared with non-migratory zebra finches and canaries.
Conditions.
Birds were exposed to dim light of 0.04 lux or to ordinary daytime room light.
Result.
Brain sections revealed Cluster N, a dorsal forebrain region.
Cluster N expression was strong at night in migrants.
Time scale.
ZENK reports activity integrated over time and does not report individual spikes.
Meaning.
Cluster N is a candidate region for night vision, with visual, magnetic or other functions possible.
Why compare species.
Non-migratory zebra finches and canaries did not show the same nocturnal increase.
Differences between species can reflect specialization for night vision.
Light levels.
Dim illumination was 0.04 lux, and daytime room illumination exceeded 275 lux.
Recent movement was minimized before tissue collection.

inserts.title: A lesion tests whether a region is necessary
paragraphs: A lesion is damage to a region of tissue made to test whether the region is needed for a behavior. A sham operation repeats the surgery without the damaging step, so differences between lesioned and sham animals can be attributed to the damage.

Zapka and colleagues injected ibotenic acid into Cluster N of European robins and tested orientation after at least 1 week of recovery. Sham birds changed direction with the rotated and inverted magnetic fields, whereas lesioned birds failed to orient coherently.

The region is therefore necessary for normal magnetic compass performance in this preparation. A necessity result identifies a stage in the pathway and does not by itself show that every neuron in the region responds to magnetic fields.
notes: A lesion removes a region to test its role.
Lesion and sham.
A lesion damages a region.
A sham operation repeats the procedure without the active injection.
Method.
Ibotenic acid was injected locally into Cluster N on both sides.
Tests followed at least 1 week of recovery.
Test fields.
The natural field was compared with a field with magnetic north rotated 120 degrees anticlockwise.
An inverted vertical component was also tested.
Sham birds.
They changed direction appropriately with the field manipulations.
Lesioned birds.
They failed to express coherent magnetic compass orientation.
Meaning.
Cluster N is necessary for the compass in this preparation, and its neurons need not all be magnetic.
Selectivity.
Lesioned birds still oriented with stars and at sunset.
The loss of orientation is therefore specific to the magnetic compass.
Inference.
Cluster N is necessary for the tested compass behavior, and the neurons that respond to magnetic fields remain to be located within the pathway.

inserts.title: Virtual displacement changes the field but not the place
paragraphs: Virtual magnetic displacement sets the local magnetic parameters to those of another place while the animal stays at its capture site. Celestial, olfactory and landmark information continue to indicate the original location. The method therefore changes only the magnetic information while the animal remains in the same place.

Pakhomov and colleagues tested Eurasian reed warblers in spring migration. The capture-site field had an intensity of 50,118 nT and inclination of 70.1°, and the replicated field from Zvenigorod, about 1,000 km east, had 52,175 nT and 71.2°.

Declination, the angle between geographical and magnetic north, also changed from +5.5° to +10.1°. A bird that compensates for the apparent eastward displacement changes its heading, which tests a map and not only a compass.
notes: A virtual displacement creates a conflict between magnetic and other location cues.
Definition.
Virtual magnetic displacement changes the local magnetic parameters to those of another place.
Other cues.
Celestial, olfactory and landmark cues stay associated with the capture site.
Capture site field.
Intensity was 50,118 nanotesla and inclination was 70.1 degrees.
Replicated field.
Zvenigorod lies about 1,000 kilometers east.
Its field had 52,175 nanotesla and 71.2 degrees.
Declination.
Declination is the angular difference between geographical and magnetic north.
It changed from plus 5.5 to plus 10.1 degrees.
Test of a map.
Compensation for the apparent eastward displacement is a map-based response and not a simple compass rotation.
Compensation.
A bird that compensates for an eastward displacement changes its heading toward the west of its capture-site course.
Sham-operated birds changed from a northeasterly course to about 323 degrees.
Role of the trigeminal nerve.
Birds with the ophthalmic branch cut maintained a course near 34 degrees and did not make the change.

inserts.title: Immunohistochemistry localizes a protein in tissue
paragraphs: Immunohistochemistry uses antibodies to label a protein in tissue sections. A fluorescent signal marks where the antibody found its target, so the method reveals which cells and compartments contain the protein. The antibodies bind to the protein only where it occurs in the tissue.

Günther and colleagues applied antibodies against Cry4 to robin retina. Cry4 immunoreactivity was concentrated in photoreceptor outer segments and appeared across peripheral and central regions, and the pattern was compared in robins and chickens with monoclonal and polyclonal reagents.

An outer segment is the compartment of a photoreceptor that contains the light-sensitive membrane. A candidate magnetic protein located there lies in a position compatible with a process that depends on light. The localization is consistent with a role in a light-dependent process in the retina.
notes: Antibody labeling shows where a protein is located in a tissue.
Method.
Antibodies bind to a specific protein in a tissue section.
A fluorescent label marks the bound antibody.
The retina.
The retina contains light-sensitive photoreceptors, including cones and rods.
Outer segments.
The outer segment is the specialized compartment that contains light-sensitive membrane structures.
Result.
Cry4 immunoreactivity was concentrated in outer segments.
It appeared across peripheral and central retinal regions.
Reagents.
Monoclonal and polyclonal reagents were both used, so the result does not rest on one antibody.
Species comparison.
The pattern was compared in robins and chickens.
Controls for the antibody.
Using different kinds of antibody reagents reduces the chance that the pattern comes from one preparation.
The staining was compared with chicken retina.
Where light is detected.
Light-sensitive membrane structures sit in the outer segment, which makes it the site of the first steps of vision.
A protein in this compartment is positioned to be exposed to light.

inserts.title: A radical pair contains two unpaired electrons
paragraphs: A radical is a molecule with an unpaired electron, and a radical pair is two such molecules produced together by a reaction. The spins of the two electrons can be correlated in a singlet or a triplet state. The photochemistry was studied in purified protein, outside the animal.

In Cry4, light-excited FAD receives an electron through a chain of tryptophan residues, which produces a radical pair. Xu and colleagues replaced individual tryptophans with redox-inactive phenylalanine and followed changes in absorption after 450-nm excitation.

Interrupted early transfer pathways produced radical-loss time constants of 180 ps and 900 ps, and longer pathways supported radicals that persisted longer. The residues in the chain therefore set the lifetime of the radical pair. Mutating a single residue can change the rate of electron transfer.
notes: The chemistry of a radical pair depends on electron spin.
Radicals.
A radical has an unpaired electron.
A radical pair contains two radicals generated through a linked reaction.
In Cry4.
Light-excited FAD receives an electron through a chain of tryptophan residues.
This produces radicals whose reactions depend on their electronic states.
Mutations.
Individual tryptophans were replaced with redox-inactive phenylalanine.
Redox refers to electron-transfer chemistry.
Measurement.
Transient absorption tracked changes over time after 450-nanometer excitation.
Result.
Interrupted early transfer pathways gave radical-loss time constants of 180 and 900 picoseconds.
Longer pathways.
Longer transfer pathways supported radicals that persisted beyond the earliest nanosecond responses.
Time scales.
A picosecond is one trillionth of a second.
The measured time constants were 180 and 900 picoseconds.
Role of the chain.
The nearest tryptophan prevented the normal radical production when it was replaced.
Longer pathways supported longer-lived radicals.
Measurements used purified protein, so the chemistry is studied outside the animal.

inserts.title: Prussian blue stains iron and not cell identity
paragraphs: Prussian blue stains a form of iron accumulation in tissue. A stained cell contains iron, but the stain does not show what kind of cell it is, so cell identity has to be established with other markers. The stain is a first step, and other markers are needed to decide what the stained cell is.

Treiber and colleagues reexamined iron-rich cells in pigeon upper beaks that had been proposed as magnetosensitive neurons. The iron-positive cells occurred in subepidermal tissue, respiratory epithelium and feather follicles.

Their positions and abundance varied strongly across birds, and at least 97% of the stained cells in the examined compartments had visible nuclei. The cells did not form the stereotyped bilateral arrangement that a sensory organ would show. The distribution of iron-positive cells was therefore inconsistent with a sensory organ.
notes: A stain that detects a material cannot identify a cell by itself.
Stain.
Prussian blue detects a form of iron accumulation.
It does not establish neuronal identity.
The proposal.
Iron-rich cells in the upper beak of pigeons had been proposed as magnetosensitive neurons.
Where the cells were.
Iron-positive cells occurred in subepidermal tissue, respiratory epithelium and feather follicles.
Variability.
Their positions and abundance varied strongly across birds.
They did not form a stereotyped bilateral arrangement.
Nuclei.
At least 97 percent of the stained cells in the examined compartments contained visible nuclei.
Meaning.
A magnetic material has to be linked to an identified sensory cell and pathway to be a receptor.
Sample details.
Iron-positive cells were examined in several compartments of the upper beak.
Their number differed greatly between individual birds.
Why the identification matters.
A receptor would need to show a consistent position and a connection to the nervous system.
